segments.narration: Rome's most notorious party town is now under the sea. Baiae, on the Bay of Naples. Its mosaic floors sit about five metres down.
Seneca called it a harbour of vice. Caesar kept a villa here. Nero built one. Hadrian died in his.
The whole town was built on hot mineral springs, and one bath dome was the widest in the world before the Pantheon. So what sank it?
Not a wave, not an earthquake. The ground itself. The volcanic field underneath breathes, lifting and dropping this coast by metres, and Baiae sat on the part that sank.
By the eighth century the lower town was sea floor. Since 2002 it is a protected park, and divers swim its streets past the emperors' floors.

verdicts.claim: Baiae was built around warm mineral springs, and the structure once called the Temple of Mercury is part of a thermal bath complex with a dome about 21.5 metres across, the largest in the world before the Pantheon.

verdicts.claim: The submersion of Baiae was caused by bradyseism, ground movement from volcanic activity in the Phlegraean Fields, which lowered the coastline in phases.
verdicts.note: 79% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The lower town was largely underwater by the 8th century, and an underwater archaeological park protecting the submerged remains was established in 2002.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives both the 8th-century submersion of the lower town and the 2002 establishment of the underwater archaeological park protecting ports, mosaics, frescoes and sculptures.
